title: Roots, plexus and nerves: the map problem
description: Every limb carries three overlapping maps. This module shows how to choose the muscle or reflex that tells them apart.
why: Root, plexus and nerve each map the same limb in a different way, so the examiner's job is to find the muscle or reflex that only one of them can explain.
objectives: Distinguish a dermatome, a myotome and a nerve territory, and explain why one root lesion may numb very little.
Apply the two rules: every muscle a nerve supplies below the lesion must be weak; test a muscle with the same root but a different nerve.
Tell a common peroneal neuropathy from an L5 radiculopathy at the bedside.
Localize a brachial plexus birth injury to the roots or the trunks using the root-level branches.
Use the tendon reflexes as root markers, and recognize the cord's lost-here, brisk-below pattern.

sections.title: Dermatomes, myotomes and nerve territories
sections.content:
Every limb is covered by three maps at once, and they don't agree with one another. The **dermatome** is the skin that a single dorsal root supplies, and the **myotome** is the set of muscles that a single ventral root supplies. The **nerve territory** is whatever one named peripheral nerve supplies after the plexus has shuffled the roots together. A root lesion stands apart from a plexus or nerve lesion because its signs follow the segments (Brazis 2011, p. 89).

**Sensory loss from a single root**

Neighboring dorsal roots overlap so much that cutting one of them causes little or no sensory loss. A normal sensory exam therefore does not exclude a root lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 89), and the motor and reflex findings deserve more trust than a numb patch. Root lesions more often show themselves through pain. The pain is sharp and electric, runs along the root's territory, and gets worse with coughing, straining or sneezing (Brazis 2011, p. 89).

**Two rules for the limbs**

The first rule is that if a nerve lesion weakens a muscle, **every muscle that nerve supplies below the lesion must also be weak**. Suppose brachioradialis is weak from a radial nerve lesion at the spiral groove. Wrist and finger extension must then be weak too. If they are not, the problem lies somewhere else (Morris 2012, p. xxix).

The second rule separates a root from a nerve. It tells you to **test a muscle with the same root but a different nerve**. Weak quadriceps could come from the femoral nerve or from the L2 to L4 roots. The hip adductors share those roots but travel in the obturator nerve, so their strength settles the question (Morris 2012, p. 23).

**In a child**

Root and nerve lesions in children are more often traumatic, compressive or present from birth than degenerative. Young children are also poor reporters of numbness. Both facts put more weight on strength and reflexes, which don't depend on the child's description. The rest of this module applies the two rules to the arm, the leg and the newborn plexus.

The dermatome map above marks the single point the international spinal cord injury standard uses to test each root, because whole dermatomes overlap too much to test reliably ([Kirshblum 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22330108/)).
keyPoints: Each limb carries three overlapping maps, the dermatome, the myotome and the nerve territory.
Cutting a single dorsal root may cause little or no sensory loss, so normal sensation does not exclude a root lesion (Brazis 2011, p. 89).
The first rule is that every muscle a nerve supplies below a lesion of that nerve must be weak (Morris 2012, p. xxix).
The second rule separates root from nerve by testing a muscle with the same root but a different nerve (Morris 2012, p. 23).
In children, the motor findings and reflexes deserve more weight than reported numbness.

question.question: A 13-year-old has weak, wasted quadriceps and an absent knee reflex after a pelvic injury. Which single test best separates a femoral nerve lesion from a lesion of the L2 to L4 roots?
options: Strength of the hip adductors, which share the roots but travel in the obturator nerve
Strength of ankle dorsiflexion
Pinprick sensation over the front of the thigh
The ankle reflex
question.explanation: The hip adductors share the L2 to L4 roots with the quadriceps but travel in the obturator nerve. Weak adductors point to the roots or plexus, and strong ones to the femoral nerve (Morris 2012, p. 23). Dorsiflexion tests L4 and L5 through the peroneal nerve. Root overlap blurs thigh sensation, and the ankle reflex runs through S1.

sections.title: Localizing weakness in the arm
sections.content:
The figure above applies the two rules for you. Mark each muscle or reflex you tested as weak or normal. The figure then keeps only the roots, plexus trunks and nerves that explain everything you found, and notes why each rejected candidate dropped out. Behind it is a table that gives each muscle its **predominant** root. Sources differ by a segment here and there, so read the table as a teaching map whose boundaries may shift by a level.

**Wrist drop**

Start with the wrist-drop preset. The wrist and fingers drop and brachioradialis is weak, but triceps and its reflex are normal. The branches to triceps leave the radial nerve high in the arm, so a normal triceps puts the lesion at or below the spiral groove of the humerus (Morris 2012, p. 11). The radial muscles below the groove are weak and those above it are spared, which is the first rule at work (Morris 2012, p. xxix). A C7 root lesion could look similar, but triceps depends mainly on C7, so a normal triceps rules the root out.

**Ulnar nerve or lower trunk**

When the first dorsal interosseous is weak and wasted, check the thumb's short abductor next. Both depend on the C8 and T1 roots, but the interosseous travels in the ulnar nerve and the thumb abductor in the median nerve. A weak interosseous beside a strong thumb abductor points to the **ulnar nerve**. Weakness in both points higher, to the lower roots or the lower trunk of the plexus. This is the second rule again, and the figure works it out for you.

**A screening sequence for the arm**

A practical sweep of the arm needs only a few muscles, each chosen because it separates the candidates.

- Shoulder abduction (axillary, mainly C5)
- Elbow flexion (musculocutaneous, C5 and C6)
- Elbow extension (radial, mainly C7)
- Wrist and finger extension (radial)
- Thumb abduction (median, mainly T1)
- Finger spreading (ulnar, mainly T1)

Then add the biceps, brachioradialis and triceps reflexes.

**In a child**

Strength testing goes better as a contest, done one side at a time so that the two sides can be compared. A child who won't cooperate with formal testing will often show you shoulder abduction, elbow extension and grip anyway while reaching for a toy held high, to the side, or just out of reach.
keyPoints: A radial nerve lesion at the spiral groove spares triceps, whereas a C7 root lesion would weaken it.
A weak first dorsal interosseous with a strong thumb abductor points to the ulnar nerve, and weakness of both points to the lower roots or lower trunk.
Test the muscles that separate the candidates rather than testing everything.
Root assignments vary by a segment between sources, and the figure uses the predominant roots.

question.question: A 15-year-old wakes with a wrist drop after sleeping with his arm over a chair back. Finger extensors and brachioradialis are weak; triceps and the triceps reflex are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: The C7 root
The posterior interosseous nerve in the forearm
The posterior cord of the brachial plexus
The radial nerve at or below the spiral groove of the humerus
question.explanation: Brachioradialis and the wrist and finger extensors are radial muscles, and triceps is spared. Its branches leave the nerve high in the arm, so the lesion is at or below the spiral groove (Morris 2012, pp. xxix, 11). A C7 lesion would weaken triceps. The posterior interosseous nerve branches after brachioradialis, and a posterior cord lesion would weaken deltoid.

sections.title: Foot drop: peroneal nerve or L5 root
sections.content:
Foot drop is the commonest focal leg problem a neurologist is asked to localize, and two very different lesions produce it. The common peroneal nerve winds around the head of the fibula just under the skin, where it is easily compressed. The L5 root supplies the same ankle dorsiflexors. It also supplies muscles that the peroneal nerve never reaches, and those muscles tell the two lesions apart.

**Inversion and hip abduction**

When dorsiflexion, eversion and big-toe extension are weak and the reflexes are normal, the lesion is in the **common peroneal nerve**. Look for scars or bruising over the fibular head. When dorsiflexion and eversion are weak **and so is inversion**, sometimes with weak hip abduction, the lesion is at the **L4/L5 root or plexus** (Morris 2012, p. 26). Tibialis posterior, the main invertor, is an L5 muscle carried by the tibial nerve. Gluteus medius, the hip abductor, is an L5 muscle carried by the superior gluteal nerve. A peroneal lesion leaves both strong, because neither belongs to that nerve.

In a patient with sciatica, weak big-toe extension may be the only motor sign of an L5 root lesion (Morris 2012, p. 29). When everything at the ankle is weak and the ankle reflex is lost, widen the search to a neuropathy, a sciatic nerve lesion, or a root or plexus lesion affecting several segments (Morris 2012, p. 26).

**Testing inversion**

Hip rotation can fake inversion. Hold the shin still with one hand, move the foot into inversion with the other, and then ask the child to hold it there (Morris 2012, p. 29).

**Using the figure**

The figure in the previous section has two foot-drop presets. Load them one after the other. In the first, inversion and hip abduction are normal, and the common peroneal nerve is the only candidate left. In the second, both are weak, and only the L5 root survives, because three different nerves are involved and the root is the one thing they share.

**In a child**

In a child, peroneal neuropathy tends to follow weight loss, a tight cast, prolonged squatting or kneeling, crossing the legs, or a knee injury. An L5 radiculopathy is unusual in a young child, so a convincing one deserves imaging to look for the cause.
keyPoints: A common peroneal lesion weakens dorsiflexion, eversion and big-toe extension while sparing inversion and hip abduction (Morris 2012, p. 26).
An L4/L5 root or plexus lesion weakens inversion as well, and often hip abduction (Morris 2012, p. 26).
Weak big-toe extension may be the only motor sign of an L5 root lesion (Morris 2012, p. 29).
Inversion should be tested with the shin held still, so that hip rotation cannot fake it.
A convincing L5 radiculopathy in a young child deserves imaging for a cause.

question.question: A 12-year-old who lost weight quickly has a foot drop. Dorsiflexion and eversion are weak; inversion and hip abduction are normal; the ankle reflex is normal. Where is the lesion?
options: The L5 root
The common peroneal nerve near the fibular head
The sciatic nerve
The tibial nerve
question.explanation: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with normal inversion and hip abduction is the common peroneal pattern (Morris 2012, p. 26), and rapid weight loss strips the fat that cushions the nerve. An L5 lesion would weaken inversion and hip abduction. A sciatic lesion usually weakens inversion, though a partial one can mimic this (Brazis 2011, p. 58). A tibial lesion spares dorsiflexion.

sections.title: The lesion ladder
sections.content:
A nerve gives off its branches in a fixed order, like the cable in this module's opening. A lesion removes every branch below it and spares every branch above. The **highest branch that is lost** places the lesion between that branch and the next one up, which still works.

**The facial nerve**

Inside the temporal bone the facial nerve gives off three branches before it reaches the face. They are the branch for tears at the geniculate ganglion, the nerve to stapedius, and the chorda tympani, which carries taste from the front of the tongue (Brazis 2011, pp. 322-323). Each branch a lesion passes on its way up the nerve adds a deficit (Brazis 2011, pp. 326-327).

- Below the chorda tympani, only the face is weak.
- Above the chorda, taste is lost as well.
- Above the stapedius branch, **hyperacusis** is added, with ordinary sounds too loud on that side.
- At or above the geniculate ganglion, a **dry eye** joins the picture.
- In the internal auditory canal, the eighth nerve rides alongside, so deafness joins too. Sources differ on whether the deafness replaces the hyperacusis or the hyperacusis can persist (Brazis 2011, p. 326; Pearl 2014, p. 51).

The figure lets you climb this ladder and the radial and foot-drop ones, and a drawing of the nerve with three marked lesion sites shows the same idea (Pearl 2014, p. 52).

**In a child**

Bell palsy is still the commonest cause, but not every facial palsy is Bell's (Brazis 2011, p. 329). Look at the middle ear in every child with facial weakness, since otitis media and mastoiditis can reach the nerve (Brazis 2011, p. 330). Where Lyme disease is common, it is the commonest cause of a bilateral facial palsy (Pearl 2014, p. 52). Elsewhere don't assume it, and keep Guillain-Barré syndrome and leukemia on the list (Brazis 2011, p. 329).

:::deeper The radial and foot-drop ladders
The radial ladder starts at the posterior interosseous branch, where the fingers drop and the wrist still extends. At the spiral groove the wrist drops as well and triceps is spared. In the axilla triceps is lost too (Brazis 2011, pp. 44-45). Absent triceps function is sometimes listed under the spiral-groove palsy (Pearl 2014, p. 83), but the triceps branches leave above the groove, so the order of the branches argues against it.

The foot-drop ladder runs from the deep peroneal branch to the common peroneal nerve and on to the sciatic, which adds inversion, plantar flexion and the hamstrings (Pearl 2014, p. 87). Hip abduction decides between the sciatic nerve and the L5 root, because gluteus medius is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, which is not on the sciatic ladder at all (Brazis 2011, p. 53).
:::

**Lesions above the nerve**

At the top of the ladder the pattern changes shape instead of growing. In the pons, a facial palsy comes with a gaze palsy and a crossed hemiparesis (Brazis 2011, p. 325). Above the nucleus, the forehead is relatively spared (Pearl 2014, p. 50). At the C7 or L5 root, muscles belonging to several nerves fail together. Each of these patterns means the lesion is no longer in the nerve itself.
keyPoints: A nerve sheds its branches in order, so the highest lost branch marks the lesion and more proximal lesions accumulate deficits.

Climbing the facial nerve from the bottom, a lesion takes the face, then taste (chorda tympani), then adds hyperacusis (stapedius), a dry eye (geniculate) and finally deafness in the canal (Brazis 2011, pp. 326-327).
Every child with facial weakness needs a look at the middle ear, because not every facial palsy is Bell's (Brazis 2011, pp. 329-330).
A radial lesion at the spiral groove spares triceps, and in foot drop hip abduction lies off the sciatic ladder (Brazis 2011, pp. 45, 53).
When the pattern stops growing and changes shape, as in the pons, above the nucleus or at a root, the lesion has left the nerve.

question.question: A 9-year-old has a right facial palsy that includes the forehead. She says the television sounds painfully loud in her right ear, and taste is lost on the right front of the tongue. Hearing is normal and tear production is equal on the two sides. Where along the nerve is the lesion?
options: Distal to the stylomastoid foramen, in the parotid
In the internal auditory canal
In the facial canal, above the nerve to stapedius but below the geniculate ganglion
In the left hemisphere
question.explanation: Hyperacusis places the lesion above the branch to stapedius, and the lost taste agrees. Equal tears place it below the geniculate ganglion (Brazis 2011, p. 326). A parotid lesion would spare taste and hearing (Brazis 2011, p. 327). A lesion in the internal auditory canal would dry the eye and usually deafen the ear. A hemispheric lesion spares the forehead.

sections.title: The brachial plexus at birth
sections.content:
A newborn whose arm lies still after a difficult delivery is a pure test of plexus localization. The baby cannot follow instructions, so everything is read from posture, spontaneous movement and reflexes.

**Erb palsy and Klumpke palsy**

In the plexus, C5 and C6 join at Erb's point to form the upper trunk, C7 forms the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 form the lower trunk (Fisch 2012, p. 30). An **upper trunk (C5, C6) lesion, Erb palsy**, usually follows shoulder dystocia. It weakens supraspinatus, infraspinatus, deltoid, biceps and supinator, so the arm hangs limply at the side, turned in and pronated (Pearl 2014, p. 80). A **lower plexus injury, Klumpke palsy**, weakens the intrinsic hand muscles and finger flexors (Pearl 2014, p. 80). Some define it as C7 to T1 (Pearl 2014, p. 80), but the lower trunk comes from C8 and T1 alone (Fisch 2012, p. 30).

**Root or trunk**

Two nerves leave the roots before the plexus forms. The dorsal scapular nerve runs from C5 to the rhomboids, and the long thoracic nerve runs from the upper roots to serratus anterior (Fisch 2012, p. 31). The suprascapular nerve leaves later, from the upper trunk (Fisch 2012, p. 35). These branches work like a ruler laid along the plexus. If the rhomboids and serratus work but the deltoid, biceps and infraspinatus do not, the injury lies beyond the roots, in the upper trunk. If they are weak too, the damage is at the roots. A Horner syndrome on the same side points to involvement of T1 near the spine (Pearl 2014, p. 80).

**Examining the newborn arm**

Watch spontaneous movement and the Moro response, which shows whether each shoulder abducts and elbow flexes ([[m02-the-exam|Module 2]]). Check the biceps reflex, which is absent in an upper trunk injury. A working grasp in an arm that otherwise hangs still shows that the lower trunk is intact. Winging of the scapula when the infant pushes against your hand means a weak serratus.

**Other causes of a still arm**

A clavicle or humerus fracture, or an infected shoulder joint or bone, can make a newborn refuse to move a painful arm. A perinatal stroke is unlikely in the first days, because it usually announces itself with seizures, and the arm weakness becomes obvious only months later. A plexus injury gives a lower motor neuron pattern in a root distribution, with the reflex lost.
keyPoints: An upper trunk (C5, C6) birth injury, Erb palsy, leaves the arm hanging at the side, turned in and pronated, with the biceps reflex absent (Pearl 2014, p. 80).
A lower plexus injury, Klumpke palsy, weakens the intrinsic hand muscles and finger flexors (Pearl 2014, p. 80).
The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves leave the roots before the plexus, so spared rhomboids and serratus place an injury beyond the roots (Fisch 2012, p. 31).
In a newborn, the plexus is read from posture, the Moro response, the grasp and the biceps reflex.
A fracture or a perinatal stroke can also make a newborn's arm lie still.

question.question: A newborn's right arm hangs at the side, turned in and pronated. The biceps reflex is absent and the Moro response shows no right shoulder abduction or elbow flexion. The hand grasps well, and there is no winging of the scapula. Where is the injury?
options: The C5 and C6 roots, torn from the cord
The lower trunk of the brachial plexus
The upper trunk of the brachial plexus (Erb palsy)
The left cerebral hemisphere, from a perinatal stroke
question.explanation: Weak shoulder abduction and elbow flexion, an absent biceps reflex and a working hand make the upper trunk pattern (Pearl 2014, p. 80). Serratus is supplied before the plexus forms, so an intact serratus puts the injury beyond the roots (Fisch 2012, p. 31). An avulsion could wing the scapula, the lower trunk carries the working hand, and a stroke would keep the reflex.

sections.title: Reflexes and their segments
sections.content:
A tendon reflex is one of the most objective tests in the limb exam, because it doesn't depend on the child's effort, cooperation or description. It tests one short loop made of a stretch receptor, a sensory fiber, one or two cord segments, a motor neuron and a muscle. A lost reflex therefore localizes better than almost any sensory complaint.

**The segments**

The table gives the values in common use.

| Reflex | Main segments | Nerve |
|---|---|---|
| Biceps | C5, C6 | Musculocutaneous |
| Brachioradialis | C6 (with C5) | Radial |
| Triceps | C7 | Radial |
| Knee | L3, L4 | Femoral |
| Ankle | S1 | Tibial |

Sources differ by a segment. The knee reflex is sometimes given as L2 to L4 and the ankle reflex as S1 to S2 (Brazis 2011, p. 117), and the figure in this module uses those wider ranges. For localization, the order of the reflexes from top to bottom matters more than exactly where each boundary falls.

**Reflexes and the level of a cord lesion**

In a cord lesion, reflexes are lost at the level of the lesion and increased below it (Brazis 2011, p. 12; Morris 2012, p. xxix). An absent biceps reflex with a brisk triceps and brisk knee and ankle jerks therefore puts the lesion in the cord at the C5 and C6 segments, a pattern that [[m06-spinal-cord|Module 6]] develops.

**Getting a reflex in a child**

To a toddler a reflex hammer looks like a weapon, so bring it out late in the exam, on the parent's lap, and turn it into a toy ([[m02-the-exam|Module 2]]). Reinforcement often brings out a reflex that seems absent. Ask the child to clench their teeth or pull their hands apart while you tap. Compare the two sides every time, because asymmetry is often more informative than the absolute grade.

**Reading a lost reflex**

An absent ankle reflex on one side, with weak plantar flexion and numbness on the outer foot, points to S1. Absent ankle reflexes on both sides with stocking sensory loss point instead to a length-dependent neuropathy ([[m04-motor-unit|Module 4]]). The reflex tells you which loop is involved, and the other findings tell you where in the loop the break lies.
keyPoints: The usual reflex segments are biceps C5 and C6, brachioradialis mainly C6, triceps C7, knee L3 and L4, and ankle S1, though sources differ by a segment.
A reflex does not depend on effort or description, so it localizes more reliably than reported numbness.
In a cord lesion, reflexes are lost at the level and brisk below it (Brazis 2011, p. 12; Morris 2012, p. xxix).
A reflex that seems absent should be reinforced, and the two sides should always be compared.
One-sided reflex loss suggests a root or nerve, while symmetric distal loss suggests a polyneuropathy.

question.question: A 16-year-old with back pain has an absent right ankle reflex, weak right plantar flexion and numbness of the outer right foot. Which additional finding would point to the S1 root rather than the tibial nerve?
options: Weak right ankle dorsiflexion
Weak right hip extension (gluteus maximus)
A brisk right knee reflex
Loss of vibration at both big toes
question.explanation: Gluteus maximus shares the S1 root but is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve, which leaves well above the tibial nerve. Weak hip extension therefore points to the root (Morris 2012, p. 23 gives this same-root, different-nerve logic). Weak dorsiflexion belongs to L4 and L5. A brisk knee reflex involves neither candidate. Lost vibration at both big toes suggests a neuropathy.

quiz.question: A 14-year-old dislocated his shoulder. He cannot lift his arm out to the side and has a numb patch over the outer shoulder; elbow flexion and the biceps reflex are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: The C5 root
The upper trunk of the brachial plexus
The axillary nerve
The suprascapular nerve
quiz.explanation: Weakness confined to shoulder abduction, with numbness over the outer shoulder after a dislocation, is an axillary nerve lesion, and the nerve's course around the humeral neck explains the injury. A C5 root or upper trunk lesion would also weaken biceps and remove its reflex, and both are normal here. The suprascapular nerve has no skin territory over the outer shoulder.

quiz.question: A 15-year-old has weak finger spreading, a wasted first dorsal interosseous and numbness of the little finger. Thumb abduction is strong. Where is the lesion?
options: The ulnar nerve
The lower trunk of the brachial plexus
The T1 root
The median nerve at the wrist
quiz.explanation: The first dorsal interosseous and the short thumb abductor share C8 and T1 but travel in different nerves, the ulnar and the median. A weak interosseous beside a strong thumb abductor therefore points to the ulnar nerve. A lower trunk or T1 lesion would weaken the thumb abductor too, since it depends mainly on T1. A median lesion at the wrist does the opposite.

quiz.question: A newborn's arm hangs limp after a difficult delivery: no shoulder abduction, no elbow flexion, absent biceps reflex. This time the scapula wings when the infant pushes against your hand. What does the winging add?
options: Nothing, since winging is common in newborns
Serratus anterior is weak, so the injury involves the roots themselves, before the plexus forms
The lower trunk is also injured
The injury is in the spinal cord
quiz.explanation: The long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior leaves the upper roots before the plexus forms (Fisch 2012, p. 31). A weak serratus therefore moves the injury from the upper trunk to the roots themselves. The lower trunk carries the hand muscles, which winging does not test. A cord lesion would not give a one-arm lower motor neuron pattern, and winging is abnormal in a newborn.

quiz.question: A 13-year-old describes electric pain shooting down the back of one leg when she coughs. Strength and reflexes are normal, and you find no sensory loss. What should you conclude about a root lesion?
options: A normal sensory exam does not exclude it, because neighboring roots overlap on the skin
It is excluded, because a root lesion always numbs its dermatome
It is excluded, because the reflexes are normal
It is confirmed, because cough-provoked pain only comes from roots
quiz.explanation: Adjacent dorsal roots overlap so much that a single root lesion may cause little or no sensory loss (Brazis 2011, p. 89). Electric pain that worsens with coughing is typical of root irritation (Brazis 2011, p. 89), but it suggests a root lesion without confirming one. Normal reflexes don't exclude it either, since an irritative lesion can spare the reflex arc.

quiz.question: A 14-year-old has a foot drop after an intramuscular injection into the buttock. Dorsiflexion, eversion, inversion and plantar flexion are weak, knee flexion is weak, and the ankle reflex is lost. Hip abduction is strong. Where is the lesion?
options: The common peroneal nerve at the fibular head
The L5 root
The tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa
The sciatic nerve in the buttock
quiz.explanation: Weakness in both the peroneal and tibial territories puts the lesion above the sciatic division, and weak hamstrings put it higher still, which fits a buttock injection (Pearl 2014, p. 87; Brazis 2011, p. 58). An L5 lesion would weaken hip abduction (Brazis 2011, p. 53) and spare the ankle reflex. Peroneal and tibial lesions each spare half the foot.

signOff: The resident localizes three focal neuropathies or radiculopathies on real patients, naming the muscle that discriminated, and a faculty member agrees.

opener.parable: Think of a nerve as a long cable with branches leaving it at known points. Damage it anywhere and every branch below that point stops working while those above carry on, so the highest branch that has failed tells you roughly where the damage lies.
opener.history: Charles Bell (1774–1842), the Scottish anatomist and surgeon, gave his name to the commonest facial palsy. The facial nerve is also the best place to see the cable idea at work, because it gives off branches for tears, for the small muscle that damps loud sounds and for taste before it reaches the face.
